deed: Kibbutz Hatzerim adopted Simcha Blass's drip irrigation and turned it into a global industry
title: Simcha Blass invented a dripper, Kibbutz Hatzerim in the Negev built Netafim around it, and drip irrigation reached the world

trailer.text: Simcha Blass, an Israeli water engineer born in Warsaw to a Jewish Orthodox family, was the chief engineer and one of the founders of the Mekorot company.
In the early 1960s he developed and patented a drip method, and the new dripper was the first practical surface drip irrigation emitter.
Netafim engineers and Rafi Mehoudar improved the dripper, and according to the Jerusalem Post, only then did the company's global success begin.
According to Ran Maidan, Netafim's CEO when interviewed in 2015, farmers who use the technology achieve on average a 50% higher crop yield with 50% lower input.

glance.value: About 110 to 150 countries, according to different sources

glance.label: Recognition
glance.value: Rafi Mehoudar was presented as an Independence Day torch lighter

paragraphs.text: According to Nati Barak of Netafim, Kibbutz Hatzerim is in the Negev desert.
Barak said that the kibbutz had poor soil, the members struggled, and the farming work was very hard.
Uri Werber, a co-founder of Netafim from the kibbutz, said that many layers of salt were found in the land.
According to TriplePundit, Hatzerim long offered Jewish pioneers the chance to build a life while minimizing financial risks, but life in the Negev was hard and frustrating.
According to Werber, the kibbutz members came to an agreement that they needed industry.
According to Barak, the original idea was meant to provide work for 14 kibbutz members.

stations.title: The engineer and the tree that grew without water

paragraphs.text: Jewage describes Simcha Blass as an Israeli water engineer and a main figure in water development in Israel.
He was the chief engineer and one of the founders of Mekorot, together with Levi Eshkol and Pinchas Sapir.
From 1948 to 1956 he was the founder and director of the governmental water institutions of the new state.
JTA notes him as an Israeli engineer who helped farmers harness the water they have.
According to JTA, Blass saw a big tree growing apparently without water.
He dug into the soil and found an onion-shaped pocket of underground water that fed the tree's roots.
The first experimental system of this type was established in 1959.
In the early 1960s Blass developed and patented the method.
The new dripper was the first practical surface drip irrigation emitter.
Werber met with Blass in 1964, and by August 1965 an agreement was signed between Blass and the kibbutz.
According to Jewage, the contract that established Netafim was signed on 10 August 1965.
According to the same source, 80% of the company was owned by the kibbutz and 20% by Blass.
According to Werber, the kibbutz made only a small initial investment.
It used an empty industrial building that already had electricity and water.
Werber said that it was the first plant in the world with drip irrigation.
In 1972 the founders of Netafim approached Rafi Mehoudar.
He had no idea that he would develop one of the most widespread irrigation technologies in the world.
According to Mehoudar, the company needed drippers that would be more resistant to pressure changes, temperature changes and clogging.
Werber said that Mehoudar brought with him drippers of higher quality.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the company's global success began only with the recruitment of Mehoudar and his knowledge.
Then-Netafim CEO Ran Maidan said: "Simcha invented the dripper, but Rafi really developed the dripper".
Mehoudar said that he has 55 different patents for drippers.
He has an independent research and development laboratory, but Netafim has the sole rights to manufacture and sell the systems he has developed.
He was presented as an Independence Day torch lighter for his work in drip irrigation.

stations.title: From farms in Israel to farms around the world

paragraphs.text: In 1967 the company made its first sales to farms in Israel, and shortly afterwards it began exporting.
According to Barak, at that time most farmers used flood irrigation or sprinklers.
Barak said that the company had to educate the market and create it.
The first customers were grape and fruit tree growers in the desert.
According to Barak, the Jewish Agency helped farmers in remote areas and cooperated with Netafim.
According to Barak, drip irrigation was first taken from Israel by researchers who were on sabbatical in Israel and saw its success.
According to Barak, the first installation in the U.S. was in June 1970, on an avocado orchard in northern San Diego County, California.
In 1981 Netafim established its first overseas subsidiary, for sales, in the U.S.
According to Werber, one of the challenges was that farmers in many cultures initially resisted a new technology in place of their traditional methods.
The Netafim website lists milestones: in 1979, a first drip irrigation system for sugar cane, and in 1985, a first system for cotton.
According to Walla, Netafim is the world's largest manufacturer of low-volume irrigation systems.
Werber claimed that no other company in Israel sells in so many countries.
According to Maidan, farmers who use the technology achieve on average a 50% higher crop yield with 50% lower input.
Barak presented evidence that drip irrigation can double the yield of crops, including tomatoes, strawberries and bitter melon.
According to TriplePundit, around 75 percent of farms in Israel now use some form of drip irrigation.
According to the same source, of all the irrigated land in the world, only 4 percent uses drip systems.
According to Barak, Netafim's largest and fastest-growing market is India.
There, he said, the average customer has two to three acres, that is, small farmers.
Barak noted that most small farmers are women, and that new technology benefits them as well.
According to Barak, in India it is the government that says it needs drip irrigation and will finance it.
According to TriplePundit, governments and microfinance programs help poor farmers obtain the systems.
According to the Times of Israel, a new Netafim website documents how the company helped the green revolution, and how countries such as India expanded their crop yields.
Rachel Shaul of Netafim asked how many companies can say that their products help tens of millions have enough to eat every day.
According to the Jerusalem Post, Werber sounded hopeful that most of the world's agriculture would switch to drip irrigation, and predicted that the lives of poor farmers would improve.
According to the case analysis of Netafim, the company provided the people of several kibbutzim with income and jobs that were not available to kibbutzim relying solely on agriculture.
According to Calcalist, Hatzerim's three main businesses are Netafim, Jojoba Israel and Negev Ecology.
The kibbutz holds a 400-hectare jojoba farm watered by drip irrigation, to produce an oil sought by cosmetics companies.
According to Calcalist, Hatzerim and another Israeli jojoba grower account for one third of the global jojoba market.

According to previously published estimates cited by Calcalist (Hatzerim declines to address the figures), in the first sale, in 2006, Hatzerim brought in the Markstone and Tene funds as partners and sold 16% of its shares for $25 million.
Later the kibbutz sold shares to the Permira fund.
Walla reported that Netafim's debt fell from $350 million in 2008 to $120 million in 2011.
According to Calcalist, the Mexican company Mexichem agreed to acquire 80% of Netafim for about $1.5 billion.
According to Calcalist, $241 million are expected to reach the kibbutz, and it will remain with 20% of the shares.

As an example of a failure, Zvika Barkai, chairman of Hatzerim's economic management, told Calcalist that the kibbutz had invested in businesses close to Netafim, among them an entire line of plastic 'do-it-yourself' products called Waternet, which was eventually closed.
According to Ben Simon in Calcalist, the cost of water did not allow the kibbutz to sell the orchards' fruit at competitive prices, and so they were uprooted.
According to estimates cited by Calcalist, in the deal in which the Permira fund bought the stakes of Markstone and Tene, the kibbutz reluctantly sold 6% of its shares for $51 million.

claims.quote: When I arrive to some village in India or in South Africa or in Colombia, and I see the poor farmers, and how their quality of life is rising

claims.text: לפי פרופ' היימר, נטפים סיפקה הכנסה ומקומות עבודה לאנשי קיבוצים, שלא היו זמינים לקיבוצים המסתמכים רק על חקלאות.
claims.quote: Netafim has provided income and jobs to the people of several Kibbutzim not available to Kibbutzim that rely solely on agriculture.

claims.text: לפי כלכליסט, שלושת העסקים העיקריים של חצרים הם נטפים, חוחובה ישראל ונגב אקולוגיה.
claims.quote: נטפים (פתרונות השקיה), חוחובה ישראל (שמן חוחובה לתעשיית הקוסמטיקה) ונגב אקולוגיה (טיפול בפסולת)

claims.text: קיבוץ חצרים מחזיק בחוות חוחובה של 400 הקטאר המושקית בטפטוף, לייצור שמן המבוקש בחברות קוסמטיקה.
claims.quote: which includes a 400-hectare jojoba farm watered by drip irrigation in order to produce an oil long coveted by cosmetics and personal care companies

claims.text: לפי כלכליסט, חצרים ומגדל חוחובה ישראלי נוסף אחראים לשליש מהשוק העולמי של חוחובה.
claims.quote: שיחד עם מגדל חוחובה ישראלי נוסף אחראי לשליש מהשוק העולמי

claims.text: לפי כלכליסט, במימוש הראשון הכניס חצרים את קרנות מרקסטון וטנא כשותפות ומימש 16% ממניותיו תמורת 25 מיליון דולר.
claims.quote: הכניס חצרים ביוזמתו את הקרנות מרקסטון וטנא כשותפות, ומימש 16% ממניותיו תמורת 25 מיליון דולר

claims.text: בעסקת 2011 מכר קיבוץ חצרים 6.5% מאחזקותיו בנטפים לקרן פרמיירה תמורת 50 מיליון דולר.
claims.quote: הקיבוץ מכר לה 6.5% מאחזקותיו בנטפים בתמורה ל-50 מיליון דולר.

claims.text: לפי כלכליסט, בעסקה עם פרמירה מימש הקיבוץ באי־רצון 6% ממניותיו תמורת 51 מיליון דולר.
claims.quote: שבה מימש הקיבוץ באי־רצון 6% ממניותיו תמורת 51 מיליון דולר

claims.text: וואלה דיווחה שהיקף החוב של נטפים צומצם מ־350 מיליון דולר ב־2008 ל־120 מיליון דולר ב־2011.
claims.quote: היקף החוב הצטמצם מ-350 מיליון דולר ב-2008 ל-120 מיליון דולר ב-2011

claims.text: חברת מקסיכם המקסיקנית הסכימה לרכוש 80% מנטפים הישראלית, חלוצת הטפטוף, בכ־1.5 מיליארד דולר, לפי דיווח כלכליסט.
claims.quote: has agreed to acquire an 80-percent stake in the Israeli drip irrigation pioneer Netafim for about $1.5 billion

claims.text: לפי כלכליסט, מתוך עסקת מקסיכם צפויים להגיע לקיבוץ 241 מיליון דולר והוא יישאר עם 20% מהמניות.
claims.quote: 241 מיליון דולר מתוכם עתידים להגיע לקיבוץ, שיישאר עם 20% ממניותיה של חברה

claims.text: לדברי ברקאי, החברה השקיעה גם בקו מוצרי פלסטיק שנסגר, ובכך נכשלה השקעה.
claims.quote: השקענו הרבה כסף, קנינו ציוד, וייצרנו מוצרים, אבל בסוף סגרנו אותו

claims.text: לפי בן סימון, עלות המים לא אפשרה מחירים תחרותיים למטעי הקיבוץ, ולכן עקרו אותם.
claims.quote: אבל עלות המים לא אפשרה למחירים להיות תחרותיים, אז עקרנו אותם.

claims.text: לדברי ברק, לנטפים 27 חברות בנות ו־4,000 עובדים ברחבי העולם.
claims.quote: We have 27 subsidiaries and 4,000 employees now all over the world.

claims.text: לפי טיימס אוף ישראל, בנטפים 3,000 עובדים, מהם 2,000 במפעלי הייצור.
claims.quote: The company has 3,000 employees, 2,000 of whom are employed in the company

claims.text: לפי וואלה, בחלוקת תמורת העסקה ייהנו 450 חברי קיבוץ חצרים.
claims.quote: החלוקה שממנה ייהנו 450 חברי הקיבוץ, צפויה להיות דיפרנציאלית

claims.text: לדברי צביקה ברקאי בכלכליסט, בקיבוץ חיים אלף איש, ו־480 חברים הם כבעלי מניות.
claims.quote: חיים פה אלף איש, 480 חברים שהם כמו בעלי מניות

claims.text: לפי TriplePundit, בלאס הקים את נטפים ב־1965 בהשקעה של קיבוץ חצרים.
claims.quote: He founded Netafim in 1965, scoring investment from Kibbutz Hatzerim.

claims.text: נתי ברק מנטפים: ההתקנה הראשונה בארה"ב הייתה ביוני 1970, במטע אבוקדו בצפון מחוז סן דייגו
